bibliography.abstract: Crime-reporting mobile applications can enhance community safety and engagement in urban areas, yet their adoption remains low, partly because developers prioritize technological features over residents' social realities. This study used an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design to identify and validate the sociotechnical factors that drive adoption. Two focus groups and an analysis of 660 app reviews revealed that users' initial sense of usefulness fades, whereas sustained engagement depends on perceived value (PV), comprising six dimensions: safety, anonymity, recency, autonomy, camaraderie, and accessibility. A survey of 505 urban residents, analyzed with PLS-SEM, validated PV as a formative higher-order construct formed by four of these dimensions (safety, anonymity, autonomy, and camaraderie). PV was the strongest predictor of behavioral intention, ahead of effort expectancy, facilitating conditions, and performance expectancy, and behavioral intention strongly predicted actual use. The model explained 75% of the variance in behavioral intention and 51% in actual use. The findings offer design principles for community-centered crime-reporting technologies.
bibliography.title: Mixed-Methods Exploration of Sociotechnical Factors to Improve Adoption of Crime-Reporting Apps in Urban Communities

en.what: An exploratory sequential mixed-methods design analyzed 660 app reviews, two focus groups, and a survey of 505 urban residents using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to understand crime-reporting app usage. The study identified perceived value as a formative higher-order construct driven by safety, anonymity, autonomy, and camaraderie. This construct served as the strongest predictor of usage intent, explaining 75% of the variance in behavioral intention and 51% of actual app use.
en.why: App designers can now prioritize specific social and psychological drivers—specifically safety, privacy controls, and community camaraderie—over traditional usability metrics like effort expectancy when attempting to retain users on civic reporting platforms.
